pr_title: Implement ZLibStream and fix SocketsHttpHandler deflate support
pr_body:
- Implements ZLibStream, exposes it in the ref, and add tests
- Fixes SocketsHttpHandler to use ZLibStream instead of DeflateStream to make HttpClient correctly support "deflate"

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/2236
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/38022
(This completes the commit from https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/2236#issuecomment-653212590.)

The tests require the updated runtime-assets test data from https://github.com/dotnet/runtime-assets/pull/87.

cc: @ericstj @carlossanlop @geoffkizer

issue_context.title: Add support for zlib data format (RFC 1950)

review_comments:
I can see that these are not supported because `DeflateStream` also does not support them. I was going to ask why they were throwing, but I assume we would've also tried to call the underlying `_deflateStream` properties if they didn't throw.
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io.compression.deflatestream.length?view=netcore-3.1
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io.compression.deflatestream.position?view=netcore-3.1
Do you think there is any compatibility issue here?  Anyone who might desire the old behavior?

It's wrong but possible. The standard has always been for the deflate-compressed content to be wrapped in a zlib wrapper, but some of the early web servers got it wrong:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/9170338/why-are-major-web-sites-using-gzip/9186091#9186091
We could make it try both, though that gets complicated.

What is the mode of failure when the server provides deflate stream instead of zlib?  Presumably there are enough servers out there providing only deflate that this bug went unfixed for some time.  I'd hate for us to break clients talking to those servers.
I guess an AppContext switch to choose one or the other wouldn't make sense here since it is specific to the web server providing the original content, but a switch to enable the fallback (if it was expensive) might be beneficial.

> What is the mode of failure when the server provides deflate stream instead of zlib?

Exception saying the data is in the wrong format / can't be decompressed

> Presumably there are enough servers out there providing only deflate that this bug went unfixed for some time.

From what I've seen, it's more that very few clients actually request deflate because there historically was such confusion about what it meant.  But, yes, it's possible someone somewhere would break.

> I'd hate for us to break clients talking to those servers.

@geoffkizer, opinions on what you'd like to see done here?

I think we should make this change. We have time in this release to see if it breaks anyone. If it does, we could add a setting or an app config switch or something. But I think that's pretty unlikely.

> From what I've seen, it's more that very few clients actually request deflate

I think it's also that you'd need to request deflate as a higher priority than gzip. I've seen clients request "gzip, deflate" or just "gzip", but almost never "deflate" or "deflate, gzip". So in practice, if you are using compression, you're almost always using gzip.
Ok, thanks for the discussion.  I'll stick with just using ZLibStream, and I've marked the PR as a breaking change just to ensure we doc this.

Got it, so folks do have a workaround by changing their requested `Transfer-Encoding` to a different spec compliant encoding.  That's better than supporting a non-compliant deflate format.  Thanks for the discussion.
Thumbs up for httpbin.org :)
For the most part, this file is just a copy of GZipStream with minor tweaks.
These tests moved from the derived types down to the base type to avoid the duplication.

Can we add a comment here about how, even though the HTTP compression scheme is called "deflate", what it really means is "zlib"? Or something like that. Otherwise it's kind of confusing why we aren't using DeflateStream here.
Yup
It almost seems like having a DelegatingStream class would be useful.

Now you know why it was top of mind for me ;-)

That said, it wouldn't help much here, as this type would still need to override most of the methods.

And on top of that, it would expose what's effectively an implementation detail into the public API surface area.  If in the future we changed the implementation to not delegate, it'd get weird.

> That said, it wouldn't help much here, as this type would still need to override most of the methods.

why?

> why?

Because it's maintaining the same semantics as GZipStream and has a ThrowIfClosed call at the beginning of most of the overrides before it calls to the delegated stream.
Why wouldn't a DelegatingStream class do the same thing?

There is a set of common stream modifiers that are useful that we should consider adding.  Delegating, Slicing, Readonly, WriteOnly, NoDispose.  I think I've written / seen most of these multiple times.  Do we have an issue?  cc @carlossanlop

> Why wouldn't a DelegatingStream class do the same thing?

Seems to me like policy we wouldn't want there.  I could be wrong.

But again, I think that's the lesser issue; making ZLibStream derive from DelegatingStream bakes that implementation detail into the public API surface area.  That seems to me very undesirable.  I'm very much in favor of adding a DelegatingStream for use in implementation, but I'm not sure how much of a place it has in public API surface area.

> making ZLibStream derive from DelegatingStream bakes that implementation detail into the public API surface area. That seems to me very undesirable. 

I get the point, but it seems unfortunate. The broader implication here is that derivation to support code reuse is not a viable approach in our public API. That kinda sucks.
